stats.line: 11% of Americans aged 18 to 24 vape, twice as many as smoke cigarettes (5.3%). 17% use some tobacco or nicotine product.
stats.mirror: You vape every day and don't call yourself a smoker.

basis.design: national household survey (NHIS)
basis.who: adults 18+, table row for ages 18 to 24
basis.n: 29,482 adults surveyed; the report doesn't say how many were 18 to 24
basis.measured: Current use = every day or some days. The quote is a table row; its columns: any tobacco 17.0%, combustible 8.5%, cigarettes 5.3%, cigars 3.1%, pipes 1.5%, e-cigarettes 11.0%. Men of all ages: 24.1% any tobacco.

stats.caveat: Nicotine pouches were not asked about, so the true share of young nicotine users is likely higher. 2021 data.

ref.cite: Cornelius ME, Loretan CG, Jamal A, et al. (2023). Tobacco product use among adults - United States, 2021. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

stats.line: 68% of US smokers want to stop, and 55% tried in the past year. Only 7.4% had recently quit.
stats.mirror: You tried to quit this year and you're back on them.

basis.design: national household survey (NHIS)
basis.who: adults who smoke cigarettes
basis.n: 33,672 adults surveyed; the report doesn't say how many of them smoked
basis.measured: Self-reported wish to quit, a quit attempt in the past year, recent quitting, and use of counseling or medication. Only 31.2% used counseling or medication when trying to quit.

stats.caveat: Cigarette smokers only; vapers and pouch users were not asked. One year's snapshot, not a lifetime.

ref.cite: Babb S, Malarcher A, Schauer G, Asman K, Jamal A (2017). Quitting smoking among adults - United States, 2000-2015. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.
ref.quote: During 2015, 68.0% of adult smokers wanted to stop smoking, 55.4% made a past-year quit attempt, 7.4% recently quit smoking

stats.line: About 2 in 3 people who smoke a first full cigarette are projected to become dependent on nicotine at some point. For alcohol it's under 1 in 4.
stats.mirror: You thought you'd only ever smoke socially.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC, two waves), survival analysis
basis.who: adults who had ever smoked a full cigarette
basis.n: 15,918 adults who had ever smoked a full cigarette; 7,320 of them became dependent
basis.measured: Age at first full cigarette and age at first meeting DSM-IV nicotine dependence (3 of 7 signs in a year). Within the first year about 2.0% were hooked; within 10 years 15.6%.

stats.caveat: A projection from what adults recalled, mostly about cigarettes. 'Dependent' means 3 of 7 signs in a year, not necessarily a pack a day.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Pérez de los Cobos J, Hasin DS, et al. (2011). Probability and predictors of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis, and cocaine: results of the NESARC. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: Lifetime cumulative probability estimates indicated that 67.5% of nicotine users, 22.7% of alcohol users, 20.9% of cocaine users, and 8.9% of cannabis users would become dependent

stats.line: Some teens lost control over smoking within 2 days of their first inhale. Half of those who lost control did so while smoking just 7 cigarettes a month.
stats.mirror: You thought a few smokes at parties could never hook you.

basis.design: cohort followed 4 years, 11 interviews
basis.who: sixth-grade students followed into their teens; 217 of them inhaled cigarettes
basis.n: 127 teens who lost control (of 217 who inhaled; 1,246 in the study)
basis.measured: First sign of lost control on the 10-question Hooked on Nicotine Checklist, and full ICD-10 dependence. 127 of 217 inhalers lost control; half of the 83 who became dependent did so by 46 cigarettes a month.

stats.caveat: One sign of lost control is not full addiction. Teens and cigarettes only; vapes were not studied.

ref.cite: DiFranza JR, Savageau JA, Fletcher K, et al. (2007). Symptoms of tobacco dependence after brief intermittent use: the Development and Assessment of Nicotine Dependence in Youth-2 study. Archives of Pediatrics & Adolescent Medicine.
ref.quote: 10% having done so within 2 days … half had lost autonomy by the time they were smoking 7 cigarettes per month

stats.line: Men who smoke have about 1.5 times the odds of erection problems of non-smokers. Men who quit: lower, about 1.2 to 1.3 times.
stats.mirror: You smoke and have had trouble in bed, and blamed nerves.

basis.design: meta-analysis of 8 observational studies; this figure comes from its 4 long-term (cohort) studies
basis.who: men aged 40 to 79 in the 4 long-term studies
basis.n: 4 long-term studies of 513 to 22,086 men each (28,586 people in all 8 studies)
basis.when: studies published 2000–2010; review searched to January 2013
basis.measured: Odds of erection problems in current and former smokers against non-smokers. The 4 case-control studies gave a higher figure (2.1), but the authors trust the long-term studies more.

stats.caveat: The men were 40 or older. Shows a link, not proof of cause. These are odds, not a simple 'X% more likely'. The paper gives two figures for ex-smokers (1.20 and 1.29).

ref.cite: Cao S, Yin X, Wang Y, Zhou H, Song F, Lu Z (2013). Smoking and risk of erectile dysfunction: systematic review of observational studies with meta-analysis. PLoS One.
ref.quote: Compared with non-smokers, the overall odd ratio of ED in prospective cohort studies was 1.51(95% CI: 1.34 to 1.71) for current smokers

stats.line: Smokers in England spend about £20.49 a week on cigarettes, £27.66 if they buy packs. Vapers spend about £6.30.
stats.mirror: You buy a pack every couple of days and never count it.

basis.design: monthly national survey (new sample each month)
basis.who: adults who smoked or used other nicotine products
basis.n: 9,655 smokers and 1,669 vapers who said what they spend (10,323 nicotine users in all)
basis.measured: Self-reported average weekly spend, adjusted for inflation. The authors put the gap between smokers and people using only vapes or NRT at about £670 a year.

stats.caveat: Averages from what people reported in England; your spend depends on how much you use and local prices.

ref.cite: Jackson SE, Tattan-Birch H, Shahab L, Brown J (2023). How has expenditure on nicotine products changed in a fast-evolving marketplace? A representative population survey in England, 2018-2022. Nicotine & Tobacco Research.
ref.quote: Smokers spent £20.49 [95% CI = 20.09-20.91] on cigarettes each week (£27.66 [26.84-28.50] … e-cigarette users spent £6.30 [5.99-6.55]

stats.line: Smokers got about 14 minutes less sleep a night, fell asleep slower and had less deep sleep. Ex-smokers slept like never-smokers.
stats.mirror: You have one before bed and wake up tired.

basis.design: sleep study within a large cohort (Sleep Heart Health Study)
basis.who: adults: 2,916 never, 2,705 former and 779 current smokers
basis.n: 779 smokers compared with 2,916 never-smokers (6,400 in all)
basis.measured: One overnight sleep recording (polysomnography) each: time to fall asleep (5.4 minutes longer), total sleep, and time in each sleep stage.

stats.caveat: One night per person; it shows a link, not proof that smoking caused it. Vapes were not studied.

ref.cite: Zhang L, Samet J, Caffo B, Punjabi NM (2006). Cigarette smoking and nocturnal sleep architecture. American Journal of Epidemiology.
ref.quote: Compared with never smokers, current smokers had a longer initial sleep latency (5.4 minutes, 95% confidence interval (CI): 2.9, 7.9) and less total sleep time (14.0 minutes

stats.line: Only 3–5% of quit attempts made with no help last 6 to 12 months. Most slips happen in the first 8 days.
stats.mirror: You quit cold turkey on Monday and smoke again by the weekend.

basis.design: systematic review (too few, too mixed studies to pool)
basis.who: smokers trying to quit without treatment
basis.n: 15 studies or study groups (a summary of 10 earlier studies, 2 more studies and 3 untreated groups); the review didn't add up the people
basis.where: The review doesn't list the countries
basis.measured: Share still not smoking 6 to 12 months after one quit attempt, and when relapse happens.

stats.caveat: This is per attempt, not per person: many people try again and succeed later.

ref.cite: Hughes JR, Keely J, Naud S (2004). Shape of the relapse curve and long-term abstinence among untreated smokers. Addiction.
ref.quote: 3-5% of self-quitters achieve prolonged abstinence for 6-12 month after a given quit attempt.

stats.line: Quitters gain 4–5 kg on average in the first year, most of it in 3 months. About 1 in 6 lose weight.
stats.mirror: You're afraid quitting will make you fat.

basis.design: meta-analysis of 62 studies
basis.who: people who stayed quit in quit-smoking trials, with or without medication
basis.n: 514 quitters without medication at 12 months, in 25 studies (1,138 more on nicotine replacement)
basis.where: 59 of 62 trials in North America, Europe or Australia
basis.measured: Weight change from quit day to 1, 2, 3, 6 and 12 months. At 12 months: 16% lost weight, 37% gained under 5 kg, 34% gained 5–10 kg, 13% gained over 10 kg.

stats.caveat: An average; it varies a lot between people. Measured in cigarette smokers in trials, not in vapers.

ref.cite: Aubin HJ, Farley A, Lycett D, Lahmek P, Aveyard P (2012). Weight gain in smokers after quitting cigarettes: meta-analysis. BMJ.
ref.quote: Smoking cessation is associated with a mean increase of 4-5 kg in body weight after 12 months of abstinence, and most weight gain occurs within three months of quitting.

stats.line: People who quit smoking rated their life and mood better than those who kept smoking, at 1 year and at 3 years.
stats.mirror: You worry life will feel empty without cigarettes.

basis.design: cohort within a randomised quit-smoking trial, followed 3 years
basis.who: adult smokers (58.2% women)
basis.n: 376 quitters vs 649 smokers at year 1; 359 vs 640 at year 3 (1,504 started)
basis.measured: Quality of life, health-related quality of life, mood, relationship satisfaction and stressful events; smoking checked by a biochemical test. Quitters also had fewer stressors by year 3.

stats.caveat: Quitters weren't chosen at random, so they may differ in other ways. Overall life rating slipped a little for everyone, but less for quitters. Marriage satisfaction did not change.

ref.cite: Piper ME, Kenford S, Fiore MC, Baker TB (2012). Smoking cessation and quality of life: changes in life satisfaction over 3 years following a quit attempt. Annals of Behavioral Medicine.
ref.quote: Compared with continuing smokers, quitters showed improved global QOL, HR-QOL, and affect at years 1 and 3 and fewer stressors by year 3.

stats.line: Among men with erection problems who quit smoking, at least 1 in 4 improved within a year. None who kept smoking did.
stats.mirror: You have erection trouble and smoke, and never linked the two.

basis.design: cohort followed 1 year
basis.who: male smokers with erectile dysfunction and no other known cause, who asked for NRT
basis.n: 118 men who quit (163 who kept smoking)
basis.measured: Erectile function score (IIEF-5) before and after one year.

stats.caveat: Small, not a trial. Older men and men with severe problems improved less.

ref.cite: Pourmand G, Alidaee MR, Rasuli S, Maleki A, Mehrsai A (2004). Do cigarette smokers with erectile dysfunction benefit from stopping?: a prospective study. BJU International.
ref.quote: After 1 year the ED status improved in > or = 25% of ex-smokers but in none of the current smokers

stats.line: As of 2015, 59.1% of American adults who had ever smoked had quit.
stats.mirror: You think almost nobody really quits smoking for good.

basis.design: national household survey (NHIS)
basis.who: adults who had ever smoked (at least 100 cigarettes in their life)
basis.n: 33,672 adults surveyed; the report doesn't say how many had ever smoked
basis.measured: Former smokers as a share of everyone who had ever smoked (the 'quit ratio'), from survey answers. A former smoker had smoked at least 100 cigarettes but did not smoke when asked.

stats.caveat: Cigarettes only, not vaping. Self-report, not checked by a test. It counts quitters of all ages, many of whom quit long ago. People in prisons, care homes or the military weren't surveyed.

ref.cite: Babb S, Malarcher A, Schauer G, Asman K, Jamal A (2017). Quitting smoking among adults - United States, 2000-2015. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.
ref.quote: As of 2015, 59.1% of adults who had ever smoked had quit.

stats.line: Half of Americans who had ever been hooked on nicotine were free of every sign of it within about 26 years. Nicotine held on longer than alcohol, weed or cocaine.
stats.mirror: You've smoked since your teens and think you're a lifer.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews; ages recalled and modelled over a lifetime
basis.who: adults who had ever been dependent on nicotine
basis.n: 6,937 adults who had ever been hooked (of 43,093 surveyed); 1,300 of them had got free
basis.measured: The age when the signs of being hooked first appeared, and the age when they finally stopped and never came back, as people recalled it. Getting free here means no signs of being hooked any more; it does not have to mean never using. Alcohol took 14 years, weed 6, cocaine 5. For nicotine, 3.0% got free within the first year and 18.4% within 10 years.

stats.caveat: The study projects that 83.7% get free at some point in life; that is a model, not a head count. People in prisons or hospitals weren't surveyed, so the real pace may be slower. Men got free more slowly than women. Mostly cigarette smokers, before vaping.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction.
ref.quote: Half of the cases of nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine dependence remitted approximately 26, 14, 6 and 5 years after dependence onset, respectively.

stats.line: In Australian studies, between 54% and 69% of ex-smokers had quit with no medicine and no professional help.
stats.mirror: You think you need patches or pills to quit.

basis.design: systematic review of 19 studies
basis.who: smokers and ex-smokers in Australia
basis.n: 19 studies; how many people: unknown
basis.measured: Share of ex-smokers who quit 'unassisted': without medicine (nicotine patches and gum count as medicine) or help from a professional. 41% to 58% of current smokers had tried to quit that way.

stats.caveat: It shows how most people quit, not that going alone works better: far more people try alone. Before vaping was common.

ref.cite: Smith AL, Chapman S, Dunlop SM (2015). What do we know about unassisted smoking cessation in Australia? A systematic review, 2005-2012. Tobacco Control.
ref.quote: Data from these studies indicated 54% to 69% of ex-smokers quit unassisted and 41% to 58% of current smokers had attempted to quit unassisted.

stats.line: Nearly half (48.6%) of English smokers and ex-smokers said their latest quit attempt began the moment they decided, with no plan. Those unplanned tries were more likely to last at least 6 months.
stats.mirror: You keep waiting for the right day to quit.

basis.design: national household survey
basis.who: smokers who had tried to quit, and ex-smokers, aged 16 and over
basis.n: 1,914 people: 918 smokers who had tried to quit and 996 ex-smokers
basis.measured: Whether the latest quit try was planned ahead or done on the spot, and whether earlier tries lasted at least 6 months. Of 191 tries made 6 to 12 months before, 50% of unplanned ones lasted 6 months, against 28.5% of planned ones.

stats.caveat: A survey, not a trial: people remembered their tries, and on-the-spot decisions may come when people are most ready. Over 611 tries up to 5 years back: 65.4% against 42.3%. It doesn't show that setting a date fails.

ref.cite: West R, Sohal T (2006). "Catastrophic" pathways to smoking cessation: findings from national survey. BMJ.
ref.quote: 48.6% of smokers reported that their most recent quit attempt was put into effect immediately the decision to quit was made.

stats.line: On their latest try, 65.3% of US smokers stopped all at once and 62.0% cut down; most (74.7%) tried several ways. Only 12.2% used prescription quit pills.
stats.mirror: You've tried cold turkey and cutting down, and neither stuck.

basis.design: national online survey, the same smokers followed over time
basis.who: adult cigarette smokers who had tried to quit in the past 3 months
basis.n: 15,943 smokers
basis.measured: Which of 10 methods they used on their latest quit try (more than one allowed). Swapped some cigarettes for vapes 35.3%, patch or gum 25.4%, help from a doctor 15.2%, a quit website 7.1%, a quitline 5.4%.

stats.caveat: These people were still smoking, so it shows what people use, not what works. An online survey of tries in the past 3 months, as people remembered them.

ref.cite: Caraballo RS, Shafer PR, Patel D, Davis KC, McAfee TA (2017). Quit methods used by US adult cigarette smokers, 2014-2016. Preventing Chronic Disease.
ref.quote: Giving up cigarettes all at once (65.3%) and reducing the number of cigarettes smoked (62.0%) were the most prevalent methods.

stats.line: In one Ontario study, the authors' best estimate was about 30 quit attempts, on average, before one lasted a year. Failing many times is normal.
stats.mirror: You've quit a hundred times and think you're the exception.

basis.design: cohort followed up to 3 years, surveyed every 6 months
basis.who: adult smokers who tried to quit
basis.n: 1,277 smokers
basis.measured: Serious quit attempts, and quits that lasted at least a year, during follow-up, turned into attempts-per-success with a life table. Other methods gave about 6, 19.6 and 142. The first try had the best odds of lasting (11%).

stats.caveat: An average pulled up by the people who struggle most; the authors note many people quit in far fewer tries. Self-report, cigarette smokers only.

ref.cite: Chaiton M, Diemert L, Cohen JE, et al. (2016). Estimating the number of quit attempts it takes to quit smoking successfully in a longitudinal cohort of smokers. BMJ Open.
ref.quote: this study suggests that a current smoker tries to quit on average 30 times or more before successfully quitting for 1 year or longer

stats.line: With varenicline, people were about 2.3 times as likely to stay off cigarettes for 6+ months as with a dummy pill.
stats.mirror: You think quit pills are for weak people.

basis.design: Cochrane review, 41 randomised trials for this comparison
basis.who: adults who smoke
basis.n: 17,395 people in 41 trials
basis.where: of the review's 68 varenicline studies: 28 in the USA, others in Canada, Europe, Asia and Australia, and 15 across several countries
basis.measured: Not smoking at 6 months or longer, checked by breath or blood test where possible; varenicline against placebo.

stats.caveat: Prescription only. Serious side effects were reported a little more often than on a dummy pill (×1.23). Mostly tested in cigarette smokers, not vapers.

ref.cite: Livingstone-Banks J, Fanshawe TR, Thomas KH, et al. (2023). Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: We found high-certainty evidence that varenicline helps more people to quit than placebo (RR 2.32, 95% CI 2.15 to 2.51; I2 = 60%, 41 studies, 17,395 participants)

stats.line: Across 22 trials, cutting down before quitting worked about as well as quitting all at once.
stats.mirror: You can't face stopping all at once, so you never start.

basis.design: Cochrane review; this figure pools 22 randomised trials
basis.who: adults who smoke and want to quit, about 23 cigarettes a day on average
basis.n: 9,219 people in 22 trials (of 51 trials with 22,509 people in the review)
basis.where: 29 of the review's 51 trials in the USA, most others in Europe and China; most recruited volunteers through ads
basis.measured: Not smoking at 6 months or longer: a plan to cut down before quitting, against quitting on a set day. Cutting down with varenicline or fast nicotine (gum, spray) may work better than cutting down alone.

stats.caveat: Moderate certainty. One large English trial (697 smokers, all given nicotine replacement and nurse support) found stopping at once did better: 22.0% against 15.5% still off at 6 months.

ref.cite: Lindson N, Klemperer E, Hong B, Ordóñez-Mena JM, Aveyard P (2019). Smoking reduction interventions for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: There is moderate-certainty evidence that neither reduction-to-quit nor abrupt quitting interventions result in superior long-term quit rates when compared with one another.

stats.line: Switching to nicotine vapes helped about 3 more people in every 100 stay off cigarettes than patches or gum did.
stats.mirror: You're thinking of swapping cigarettes for a vape to quit.

basis.design: Cochrane review; this figure pools 9 randomised trials
basis.who: adults who smoke
basis.n: 2,703 people in 9 trials (of 104 studies with 30,366 people in the review)
basis.where: Of the review's 104 studies, 48 were in the USA and 21 in the UK; most others in Europe
basis.measured: Not smoking cigarettes at 6 months or longer: nicotine vapes against nicotine replacement such as patches and gum. As a ratio, about 1.55 times as many quit.

stats.caveat: It counts people off cigarettes, not off nicotine: many may still vape. Tested in smokers, not in people who only vape.

ref.cite: Lindson N, Livingstone-Banks J, Butler AR, McRobbie H, Bullen CR, Hajek P, et al. (2025). Electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: In absolute terms, this might translate to an additional three quitters per 100 (95% CI 2 to 5 more).

stats.line: In 2 small trials, varenicline (a quit-smoking pill) helped about 2.7 times as many people quit vaping as a dummy pill.
stats.mirror: You switched to vaping and now can't quit that either.

basis.design: Cochrane review, kept up to date; this figure pools 2 randomised trials
basis.who: people who vape nicotine
basis.n: 315 people in 2 trials (of 15 studies with 5,800 people in the review)
basis.where: 14 of the review's 15 studies were in the USA, 1 in Italy
basis.measured: Not vaping at 6 months or longer, varenicline against placebo. Text-message programs may help 13- to 24-year-olds a little (×1.32); nicotine patches plus gum showed no clear benefit.

stats.caveat: Low certainty: only 2 small trials, and the true effect could be as small as ×1.3. Prescription only.

ref.cite: Butler AR, Lindson N, Livingstone-Banks J, Notley C, Turner T, Rigotti NA, et al. (2025). Interventions for quitting vaping. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: When compared to placebo, varenicline increased vaping cessation rates at six months, but evidence was of low certainty due to imprecision (RR 2.71, 95% CI 1.33 to 5.49

stats.line: Being paid or rewarded for staying off cigarettes made people about 1.5 times as likely to still be off 6 months or more later.
stats.mirror: You'd quit faster if something real was on the line.

basis.design: Cochrane review; this figure pools 39 randomised trials
basis.who: adults who smoke (not pregnant), in workplaces, clinics and communities
basis.n: 18,303 people in 39 trials
basis.where: 33 of the review's 48 trials were in the USA, most others in Europe
basis.measured: Not smoking at the last check, 6 months or later: cash, vouchers, or money people put down themselves and won back, against no rewards. Leaving out trials still paying at that check: ×1.46, so the gain lasted after rewards stopped.

stats.caveat: In most trials a program ran the rewards and checked people's breath or urine. A private bet with a friend was not what was tested.

ref.cite: Notley C, Gentry S, Livingstone-Banks J, Bauld L, Perera R, Conde M, Hartmann-Boyce J (2025). Incentives for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: The pooled RR for quitting with incentives at longest follow-up (six months or more) compared with controls was 1.52 (95% CI 1.33 to 1.74

stats.line: Nicotine patches, gum, lozenges, sprays or inhalers made people about 1.55 times as likely to stay off cigarettes for 6+ months as a dummy product or none.
stats.mirror: You tried a patch once, felt nothing special, and gave up on it.

basis.design: Cochrane review, 133 randomised trials
basis.who: adults motivated to quit, mostly smoking 15+ cigarettes a day
basis.n: 64,640 people in 133 trials
basis.measured: Not smoking after at least 6 months, any form of NRT against placebo or no NRT. Patch 1.64, gum 1.49.

stats.caveat: Compared with placebo or no NRT, in people who mostly smoked 15+ a day. Not tested here in vapers or pouch users.

ref.cite: Hartmann-Boyce J, Chepkin SC, Ye W, Bullen C, Lancaster T (2018). Nicotine replacement therapy versus control for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: The RR of abstinence for any form of NRT relative to control was 1.55 (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.49 to 1.61).

rejected.claim: Page number '×2.3 the odds of quitting with varenicline' (existing).
rejected.why: Number checks out, word does not: 2.32 is a risk ratio, not odds. Correct: 'about 2.3 times as likely to quit' (still off cigarettes at 6+ months).

rejected.claim: Share of young US adults who use nicotine pouches.
rejected.why: No official adult figure fetched: SAMHSA's NSDUH pages returned 403 and the CDC adult survey did not ask about pouches. Only a preprint (medRxiv) found. CDC youth figure: 2.4% of high school students (2024).

rejected.claim: 22.3% of US 18–25-year-olds vaped nicotine in the past month (NSDUH 2025).
rejected.why: Seen only in a search snippet; the SAMHSA PDF returned 403, so it was not fetched.

rejected.claim: Two-thirds to three-quarters of ex-smokers quit unaided.
rejected.why: Not fetched from a primary source. Used instead: only 31.2% of US smokers used counseling or medication when trying to quit (CDC, 2015).

rejected.claim: Nearly 9 in 10 adults who smoke daily first tried smoking by age 18.
rejected.why: On a CDC page (fetched), but it names no survey, year or sample, so the basis cannot be filled. Left out.

rejected.claim: Quitting lowers anxiety and depression (Cochrane 2021, 102 studies, 169,500 people).
rejected.why: Verified (Taylor 2021, PMID 33687070), but effects are standardised scores that don't turn into plain numbers; file 02 already has the 2014 version.

rejected.claim: A year after quitting, quitters report no significant craving (572 smokers).
rejected.why: Verified (Schlam 2012, PMID 22865499) but cut to stay at 14; no number to show.

rejected.claim: Two-thirds to three-quarters of ex-smokers quit unaided (Chapman & MacKenzie 2010, PLoS Medicine).
rejected.why: Now read in full: it is a policy essay quoting older US surveys, not a study. Smith 2015 (19 Australian studies, 54% to 69%) used instead.

rejected.claim: Abrupt quitting beat gradual: 22.0% vs 15.5% off at 6 months (Lindson-Hawley 2016, 697 English smokers).
rejected.why: Verified (PMID 26975007). Shown only in the caveat of the 22-trial Cochrane review, which found the two ways about equal; the cautious pooled result leads.

rejected.claim: Unplanned quit attempts lasted 6+ months more often in the US too: 71.7% vs 45.6% (Ferguson 2009, 1,700 people).
rejected.why: Verified (PMID 19509277); agrees with the English survey already shown, so left out to avoid repeating.

rejected.claim: Feeling confident before a quit try predicts success, but only a little (Gwaltney 2009, 54 studies).
rejected.why: Verified (PMID 19290690), but the size is in standard-deviation units that don't turn into a plain number.
